input: After the initial arrival reading was discarded because the cuff was slipping, repeat measurements over several visits were reviewed by the treating doctor, who documents persistent BP 170/100 mmHg with the correct cuff and seated rest; the driver has no current cardiac symptoms, and a depot worker's much higher figure belongs to another person rather than a second measurement of this driver.

The audiologist's current signed report documents an unaided better-ear average of 37 dB over 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 kHz, with no aid worn during the measurements and audiometry explicitly completed; the driver sometimes turns the volume up for traffic updates in a noisy loading area, but the nurse separates that environmental complaint from the identified ear, frequencies and unaided testing conditions in the report.

The current physician assessment explicitly describes the driver with established diabetes as acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes, after vomiting and a measured glucose of 24 mmol/L prompted urgent assessment; the driver says the nausea eased after fluids, but the signed current review has not documented resolution of the instability, and a normal measurement copied from an earlier well visit is not evidence of the present metabolic state.

The specialist's signed history confirms two blackouts separated by more than 24 hours, with the last event 9.99 years ago and the mechanism still undetermined after completed investigations; the driver has had no more recent confirmed events, but the two episodes were not merely clustered in one day, and a family account that calls them one illness does not change the documented separation or the elapsed interval.

The discharge summary confirms a severe hypoglycaemic event 2 weeks ago in a driver with insulin-treated diabetes, when confusion prevented self-treatment and another person had to give assistance, with contemporaneous glucose of 2.2 mmol/L; the nurse records the event and interval from the signed document, while a later glucose of 6.1 after treatment and the driver's improved appearance today do not erase the documented recent severe episode or supply a specialist return-to-driving assessment.

The current ophthalmologist's signed examination confirms non-physiological diplopia within 10 degrees of central fixation, reproduced during the assessment even though the driver says the two overlapping road-sign images sometimes merge after blinking; an older note reported comfortable reading at a desk, but that earlier description neither contradicts the current reproduced double vision nor establishes that a patch or new lenses have resolved it.

The audiologist reports an unaided better-ear average of 58 dB over 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 kHz and confirms that the hearing standard is not met with the currently fitted aid; the driver says speech is louder but less clear when the reversing alarm sounds, and the completed specialist letter recommends further individual assessment without supplying a practical driver assessment result or a finding that the present equipment resolves the functional difficulty.
